text:
Marathon Petroleum has fallen about 2% over the past week, with today's small decline continuing a downward trend that started after mid-October. The immediate pressure seems to come from broader refinery economics: while crude oil prices have climbed sharply (Brent at $116, US oil at $108), refineries are already running at 93.4% capacity with gasoline and diesel inventories elevated at 205 million and 104 million barrels respectively. When refineries can't run much harder and inventories are building, refiners' profit margins tend to narrow even as oil prices rise—they're paying more for crude but can't push through enough additional volume to offset it.

The escalating Middle East tensions (Iran-backed Houthi attacks, Trump's rhetoric on Iran, and Saudi interceptions) have driven oil prices higher, but this is actually a mixed signal for a refiner. Geopolitical oil spikes tend to be temporary and can create refining headwinds if they don't translate into sustained demand—right now the data shows inventory builds, not drawdowns, suggesting the market isn't burning through product faster despite higher crude costs.
